name: Zane Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Zane, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy chargers, cables, memory cards and phone cases for Voltline Distribution, which supplies small phone shops and market stalls. The factories are mostly overseas, so my day starts early with messages and ends late with time-zone calls. I use an AI assistant for most of the paperwork, like comparing quotes, checking specs and drafting the messages, and I run a few spreadsheet macros of my own. I'm still junior after four years, because I came here late after a long run in warehouse and van work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel when people ask if you're okay with the new software?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy finding a good deal and cracking a problem, like a supplier who changes the cable spec without telling anyone. What wears me out is that I'm the oldest by twenty years on the team. Priya (the operations head) is great, but people half my age keep asking if I'm okay with all the new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fair enough, and I'd keep using what works. To friends I'd say the hype is half marketing, but there's something real in it. Online I'd write one or two posts about what the tools actually do well and do badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine with it. If nothing big happens, I stay the guy who's good at the tools and the job stays safe enough. What still gets me is the money, since I have under a month's worth saved and low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant and extend my spreadsheet macros so they flag late orders. I'd start a small side hustle buying broken phones and fixing them to sell, because I've got the bench skills from the warehouse days. And I'd save 100 a month, which is what we can spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. I'm not worried about work, but I'm not relaxed about money. It's a steady hum rather than a scare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side hustle bring in, and how much time would it take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marisol, my partner, works as a teaching assistant and her wages are modest. We're not in trouble, but one big bill like the car's gearbox could tip us into borrowing. That is the thing I'd say keeps me awake, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one big bill could tip you into borrowing. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say the plateau suits me because I know the ground. I've built my routine around what exists now. If it doesn't change much, I just carry on and get slightly better each year.

say: I'd say **fair enough** and keep using what works.
I'd tell friends the hype is half marketing, but there's **something real** in it.
think: I'm fine with it, because I'd stay the guy who's **good at the tools**.
The **money** still gets me, with under a month saved and low pay.
do: **Extend** my spreadsheet macros so they flag late orders.
**Start** a side hustle fixing and selling broken phones.
**Save** 100 a month, which is what we can spare.
feel: **Okay**, with a steady hum of money worry rather than a scare.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about work, but I'm not relaxed about money.
fieldNote: Comfortable with the tools and his job; the **money** is the live issue.
Has real bench skills from older jobs, which make the phone-repair side hustle plausible.
Plateau suits him because he knows the ground and gets better each year.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for quotes and supplier messages
Extend my spreadsheet macros so they flag late orders
Buy broken phones, fix them and sell them on weekends
Save 100 a month for the car and boiler bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's get ahead of it, and I'd offer to show people the tricks I've learned. To friends I'd say it's a real change, but it isn't the end of work. Online I'd share the way I use the tools, since it helps others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, buying desks are exactly what shrinks. But I'd be one of the ones who knows how to run the tools, so I think I'd be among the last to go. Even so, with low pay and a short list of nearby jobs, last isn't the same as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer Priya to automate the repetitive quoting and reorders myself, so my value is in running it. I'd take an online course in supply-chain analytics at night, which I can do cheaply. And I'd grow the phone repair side, with a target of 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Change like this is a good wave if you can surf it, and a bad one if you can't. I think I can. But it's a lot to carry at 58, and I'd be lying if I said I wasn't a bit tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you help, and what would you show them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lars, who sits next to me, is 26 and doesn't trust the assistant. I'd show him how I check its figures against the factory quotes. It helps him and it helps me, because people who can use these tools safely are what the firm needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Callum about his courier work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd tell my son Callum, who is a courier, is to start learning to repair things or code. He's got maybe fifteen years, but the courier job is on a clock. I'd pay for his first course if I could.

say: I'd say let's get **ahead of it** and offer to show people the tricks I've learned.
I'd tell friends it's a real change but **not the end**.
think: Buying desks shrink, but I know the tools, so I'd be among the **last to go**.
With low pay and few nearby jobs, last isn't the same as **safe**.
do: **Offer** Priya to automate the repetitive quoting and reorders myself.
**Take** a cheap night course in supply-chain analytics.
**Grow** the phone repair side towards 300 a month.
feel: Like a **wave** that's good if you can surf it, but tiring at 58.
S1.quote: Change like this is a good wave if you can surf it, and a bad one if you can't.
fieldNote: His plan is to become the **operator** of the new system, which is the most reliable protection in the job.
Still anxious because pay is low, cushion is thin and local buying jobs are few.
Helps Lars with the tools; generous, and aware it helps his own case.

steps.text: Offer Priya to automate the quoting and reorders and run the system myself
Take a cheap night course in supply-chain analytics
Grow phone repair sales towards 300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be honest about what's coming and plan together. To friends I'd say governments should have had a plan yesterday. Online I'd post something plain: ordinary families need an income guarantee, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my skills don't matter if AI does the whole thing for less. I'd be a person who is good at using tools that no longer need me. Two years is short, and my cushion is under a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ramp up the phone repairs straight away and try to earn 600 a month by the end of the year. I'd tell Marisol that we're going to a bare-bones budget, with no takeaways, no streaming and one car. And I'd look at working in the warehouse again, which is hands-on and has three more years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at the edge of a swimming pool in the dark. I know the water's there and I can swim, but I don't know how deep it is. Fear and excitement, in not-quite-even amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Ines, who's a nurse, that her job is safer than most and that she shouldn't worry about us. She'd worry anyway. I'd also ask her whether the hospital has any support or portering jobs for someone with my background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first, and how would you handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the first bill that goes unpaid would be the credit card minimum. I'd rather pay the rent and the electricity and take the hit on the card. I'd call the card company early and explain, since I've learned that beats going quiet.

say: I'd say **let's be honest** about what's coming and plan together.
I'd post that ordinary families need an **income guarantee**, now.
think: My skills don't matter if AI does it all **cheaper**.
Two years is short, and my cushion is under **a month**.
do: **Ramp** up phone repairs to earn 600 a month by year end.
**Move** to a bare-bones budget with one car and no streaming.
**Look** at warehouse work, which gets three more years.
feel: Like standing at the edge of a **dark pool**, with fear and excitement mixed.
S2.quote: I'd be a person who is good at using tools that no longer need me.
fieldNote: Skills don't save him: he sees that being **good at the tools** only helps if humans are still needed.
Acts fast on income and spending, then turns to hands-on work for the extra years.
Handles debt by calling early, a lesson from experience.

steps.text: Push phone repairs to 600 a month by year end
Go to one car and drop takeaways and streaming
Look for warehouse work, which robots reach three years later
Ask my daughter Ines about portering jobs at her hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to shape what we do. I'd tell Priya that Voltline should plan the buying desk's future now. To friends I'd say start doing the things you'd regret not doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd manage. I'd be 63, still using the tools, and probably already running a bigger side income. It's not secure, but it's not hopeless either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to get a proper chunk of savings, say three months, by the end of year two. I'd turn the phone repair side into a registered small business with a stall at the weekend market. And I'd keep sharpening my skills with the tools so I'm always the one that people turn to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a countdown with enough time on the clock. Not scary, but not comfortable either. I think the worry is that things move faster than the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming after the thinking AI gives people in hands-on jobs a few more years. I'd lean on my bench skills and the repair work as the physical part of my income. I'd feel safer with one foot in each world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Marisol decide about moving to a smaller flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marisol that if the buying desk goes, we can live on her wage plus the repair stall. We'd need to move to a smaller flat. She'd hate that, but she'd say it's better than the alternative.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to shape what we do.
I'd tell friends to start doing what they'd **regret** not doing.
think: I think I'd **manage**, still using the tools and with a bigger side income.
It's not secure, but it's **not hopeless** either.
do: **Build** three months of savings by the end of year two.
**Register** the phone repair as a small business with a weekend stall.
**Keep** sharpening my skills with the tools.
feel: Like a **countdown** with enough time on the clock, but not comfortable.
S3.quote: I'd feel safer with one foot in each world.
fieldNote: Plans a **dual** life, tools at work and bench skills on the side, using the robot delay.
Anxious because pay is low and savings are almost nothing now.
Discussing the smaller flat with Marisol shows the plan is a household one.

steps.text: Build three months of savings by the end of year two
Register the phone repair as a small business with a weekend stall
Keep up with every new AI tool Voltline adopts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's time to do it properly, and I'd offer to lead a training group. To friends I'd say don't wait, because ten years is shorter than it feels. Online I'd keep posting about practical ways to work with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 by then, so it mostly lands after my working life. I think I'd be okay. It might affect my kids more, and that's what I'd think about on a quiet night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65 and save a bit each month, aiming for a proper cushion of six months by 60. I'd keep the repair side going, because I enjoy it. And I'd help my son Callum move from courier work into something that needs more skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm enough. It's like watching a big storm on the weather map when you're still safe indoors. I'd keep an eye on it but I wouldn't be rushing around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to help your son Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum has been talking about retraining as a phone-and-laptop repair tech. I'd suggest he work a few weekends on my stall to see if he likes it. That seems more useful than any lecture from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you enjoy more if you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The way ten years changes my approach is that I can enjoy things. In the two-year picture, I'd be in survival mode, but here I can learn, save and try new things without being scared.

say: I'd say there's time to do it **properly** and offer to lead a training group.
I'd tell friends **don't wait**, because ten years is shorter than it feels.
think: It mostly lands after my working life, so I'd be **okay**.
It might affect my **kids** more, and that's what I'd think about at night.
do: **Work** until 65 and aim for a six-month cushion by 60.
**Keep** the repair side going because I enjoy it.
**Help** my son Callum move into more skilled work.
feel: **Calm enough**, like watching a storm on the weather map from indoors.
S4.quote: In the two-year picture, I'd be in survival mode, but here I can learn, save and try new things without being scared.
fieldNote: The decade lets him treat the change as something to **learn from**, not survive.
Uneasy rather than calm: thin savings now and kids' futures on his mind.
His help for Callum is practical, with a few weekends on the stall.

steps.text: Work until 65 and build a six-month cushion by 60
Keep the phone repair side going for the pleasure of it
Let Callum try a few weekends on my stall before he retrains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though it's not about the tools. I'm good with the tools. It's that I'd have almost no cash in two years, and everyone else would be fighting for the same few jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that older people who use the tools get ignored in these stories. We exist. I'd love someone to count how many of us are already doing it, instead of assuming we're all stuck.

headlineQuote: Older people who use the tools get ignored in these stories. We exist.
portrait: Zane is 58, a junior buyer at **Voltline Distribution**, who came late to the desk after years in warehouse and van work.
He is **adaptive**: he uses AI daily, writes his own spreadsheet macros and shows younger colleagues how to check the tools.
He is a **centrist** and pragmatic, with no one to blame, and he keeps looking for work-around options.
His main fix is a **side income** fixing phones, with a bench skill that robots would reach later.
He moves from uneasy to alarmed to uneasy as the date moves from never to 2028 to 2036.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because his cushion is under a month and good tool skills may not be needed.
whatWouldHelp: A **cash cushion**, paid courses for older workers, and a fair count of older people who already use AI.
